attribution.note: Marcus's own judgment of Altman's quoted promise. The paraphrase of Altman is context; the implausibility verdict is Marcus's.

semantics.note: 'Not plausible anytime in the next couple decades' is a firm dismissal, not a graded hedge, so it reads as a forecast that AI will not discover all of physics in about 20 years. The coherence part is evaluative and the contract rightly leaves it out.

contract.note: Setting the deadline at 2044 and requiring broadly accepted, comprehensive resolution is an ordinary plain reading. The early-resolution rule only allows contradiction, which is fair.

evidence.note: OpenAI's own disclosure of a mathematical proof (Yang–Mills existence) that has not been independently validated. Even if it holds, it is a single result, not all of physics, so the early-resolution rule is not met.
Preprint describing AI-assisted physics advances and the difficulty of verifying them. It does not settle the forecast.

reviews.rationale: The deadline is about June 2044, after the evaluation date. No conclusive event has occurred: OpenAI's claimed proof is a single, unvalidated company disclosure and comes nowhere near discovering all of physics. The forecast cannot be scored yet.

attribution.note: Marcus's own assertion in his own post.

semantics.note: Faithful to the three present-tense limitation claims. Leaving out 'just as I anticipated' and the 'dud' remark is appropriate.

contract.note: The first-half-2024 window and reading 'boneheaded' as elementary errors are ordinary plain readings. They are not stretched for or against the speaker.

evidence.note: June 2024 preprint finds frequent failures by leading LLMs on a simple sibling-counting problem, delivered with confident but nonsensical explanations.

Stanford's preregistered study (May 2024) finds substantial hallucination in commercial legal AI tools and in GPT-4. That the tools improved on GPT-4 does not undercut the claim that they still hallucinate.

reviews.rationale: Two independent evaluations from the period show prominent systems repeatedly hallucinating and making elementary reasoning errors that matter for dependable use. The partial improvement in e2 does not meet the contradiction condition.
